visual_base.visual_narrative_log: (1) A man with short dark hair wearing a black t-shirt stands in front of a dark, minimalist background. He addresses the camera directly with a friendly and inquisitive facial expression. Above him, bold red and yellow text overlays appear, framing the central question of the video. The lighting is bright and focused on his upper body, creating a clear studio-like atmosphere. (2) The scene transitions to a white, circular cartoon character with an exaggerated angry expression, wide eyes, and an open mouth. Beside it, the word 'Why?!' appears in a stylized font. The background is simple and graphic, emphasizing the character's reaction. (3) A hand-drawn sketch appears, showing a simple white figure sitting at a wooden desk and drawing on a piece of paper. The setting is an indoor room with a bookshelf and a plant in the background, drawn in a clean, black-and-white line art style. (4) The camera zooms into close-ups of various hand-drawn faces. Each face depicts a different exaggerated emotion: one with a tongue sticking out and squinted eyes, another with wide, shocked eyes, and one with a focused, furrowed brow. The artist's hand is visible holding a digital stylus, actively sketching these features. (5) The man returns to the screen, gesturing with his hands as he continues the explanation. In a split-screen or overlay, an animated character with green hair is shown on a computer monitor, mirroring the facial expressions discussed. The lighting remains consistent and bright. (6) A series of educational graphics appear, featuring a pink brain icon and blue silhouettes of people. One silhouette is shown mirroring the actions of another, illustrating the concept of neural reflection. The graphics are colorful and use flat animation styles to convey complex ideas simply. (7) The final phase shows black-and-white archival photographs of men in mid-20th-century attire. They are sitting at animation desks, holding mirrors and making exaggerated, funny faces at themselves while sketching. These historical images provide real-world evidence for the psychological phenomenon being described.
visual_base.text_narrative_log: (1) [Logo]: 維斯維. [Slogan]: 你畫畫時會模仿人物表情嗎？. (2) [Variety]: Why?! [Subtitle]: 畫畫的人是不是都這樣奇怪？. (3) [Subtitle]: 在畫人時，是不是常常會不小心模仿畫中人物的表情呢？. (4) [Subtitle]: 就像這樣，這樣，還有這樣。. (5) [Subtitle]: 相信不少畫畫的人都有這樣的經歷吧。我自己在製作影片繪圖時就有這樣的現象。. (6) [Subtitle]: 都是突然回神發現我剛剛的表情太奇怪了吧。為什麼會這樣啊？. (7) [Subtitle]: 這可能跟我們大腦的鏡像神經元有關。. (8) [Subtitle]: 鏡像神經元的功能就像鏡子一樣把看到的情況反射在大腦中進而模仿別人的行為。. (9) [Subtitle]: 聽說以前迪士尼動畫師在畫角色時自己也會跟著瞇眼、皺眉、扮鬼臉讓角色的表情更加生動喔。

The narrator's voice shifts to a slightly more inquisitive and playful inflection while the background music maintains its consistent rhythmic pulse. (3) The audio track features a subtle 'whoosh' sound effect transition as the visual switches to the drawing desk. The narrator continues his steady delivery, explaining the drawing process. The BGM remains in the background, providing a cheerful and energetic foundation for the speech. (4) Rapid digital 'click' sound effects occur as the different facial sketches are highlighted. These SFX are synchronized with the visual cuts, increasing the perceived editing pace. The narrator's pitch rises slightly during the examples, adding emphasis to the humorous nature of the mirrored expressions. (5) As the explanation of mirror neurons begins, a light 'sparkle' or 'magic' synthesizer flourish is added to the audio mix. The narrator adopts a slightly more informative yet still engaging tone, with the BGM volume dipping slightly to ensure the technical terms are clearly audible. (6) In the final segment, the audio maintains the established BGM. The narrator's tone becomes reflective and conclusive as he mentions the historical Disney animators. A final 'ding' sound effect marks the end of the narrative, leaving the BGM to fade out briefly.

narrative_and_purpose.narrativeStructure: List-based: Hook -> Problem -> Explanation -> Historical Evidence -> Conclusion
narrative_and_purpose.mainPurpose: The video aims to explain the psychological phenomenon where artists subconsciously mimic the facial expressions of the characters they are drawing. It utilizes the concept of 'mirror neurons' to provide a scientific basis for this common artistic experience and validates it with historical examples from professional animation history.
